title: Directions and Distance Reasoning — Part 4 of 10

questions.question: What is an 'unknown distance' problem?
options: A problem with no possible solution
A question where the distance between two points must be derived from other given relationships, rather than being stated directly
A problem that only involves direction, never distance
A problem where the distance is always zero
questions.rationale: In an unknown-distance problem, the distance isn't given directly — it must be deduced by reasoning through the other stated relationships.

questions.question: What is a 'spatial graph' used to represent?
options: Only a single point
Entities and their spatial relationships (direction/distance) as nodes and edges, similar to other reasoning graphs
A graph of elapsed time
A list of compass directions only
questions.rationale: A spatial graph models entities as nodes and their spatial relationships as edges, mirroring the node-and-edge approach used for family and temporal graphs elsewhere in reasoning.

questions.question: What does 'coordinate propagation' mean?
options: Deleting a point's coordinates
Calculating a new entity's coordinates by applying a known direction and distance from an already-positioned entity
Converting coordinates into text
Ignoring distance when placing a new point
questions.rationale: Coordinate propagation derives a new point's coordinates by applying a stated direction and distance relative to a point whose coordinates are already known.

questions.question: Why might a problem describe 'multiple entities' and their relationships rather than just two?
options: To make the problem shorter
To require chaining several spatial relationships together to determine an unknown position or distance
Multiple entities are never used in these problems
Because only two entities can ever be related
questions.rationale: With multiple entities, you often need to chain several known relationships together step by step to determine an unknown position or distance.

questions.question: What is a 'spatial constraint'?
options: A physical wall in a diagram
A stated relationship (direction, distance, or relative position) that any valid solution must satisfy
A limit on how many entities a problem can have
A synonym for displacement
questions.rationale: A spatial constraint is a given relationship — direction, distance, or relative position — that the final solution's positions must be consistent with.

questions.question: What does 'constraint solving' involve in spatial reasoning?
options: Ignoring constraints that seem irrelevant
Finding a set of positions consistent with every given spatial constraint simultaneously
Solving only the first constraint given
Randomly guessing positions until one works
questions.rationale: Constraint solving means finding positions for all entities that satisfy every given spatial constraint at once, not just some of them.

questions.question: How can direction be derived 'from angle' between two points?
options: It cannot be derived this way
By converting the angle formed by their coordinate difference into a compass direction or bearing
By measuring the time between them
By counting the number of entities involved
questions.rationale: The angle formed by the coordinate difference between two points can be converted directly into a compass direction or numeric bearing.

questions.question: What are 'polar coordinates'?
options: A coordinate system using only x and y values
A coordinate system defining a point by its distance from an origin and an angle, rather than by x/y coordinates
A synonym for Manhattan distance
Coordinates that only work near the North or South Pole
questions.rationale: Polar coordinates define a point using a distance from a fixed origin and an angle, rather than the perpendicular x/y offsets used in Cartesian coordinates.

questions.question: What is the key difference between 'Cartesian' and 'polar' coordinates?
options: They are the same system with different names
Cartesian uses perpendicular x/y axes; polar uses a distance and angle from a fixed origin point
Polar coordinates cannot represent negative distances
Cartesian coordinates only work in 3D
questions.rationale: Cartesian coordinates locate a point using perpendicular x/y axes, while polar coordinates locate the same point using a distance and an angle from an origin.

questions.question: Why might polar coordinates be more natural for some direction-and-distance problems than Cartesian coordinates?
options: They never are — Cartesian is always better
Because such problems are often stated directly in terms of a direction (angle) and a distance, matching the polar form more closely
Because polar coordinates don't require an origin
Because polar coordinates are only used for time, not space
questions.rationale: Since many direction-and-distance problems are phrased directly as 'X km in direction Y,' that maps naturally onto the distance-and-angle structure of polar coordinates.
